evidence.agreementDetail: Interviews move the third candidate's share +0.2 points (+0.2 to +0.2); the closest historical cases moved it +0.1 ± 2.0.

findings.claim: Birney won about 62,000 free-state votes in 1844, nearly ten times 1840. Polk carried New York and Michigan without majorities; if all Liberty voters there had backed Clay he would have won both and the presidency.

sources.title: Liberty Party (United States, 1840)

findings.claim: Johnson argues most Liberty voters saw Whigs as no less proslavery than Democrats and probably would not have voted Clay. Birney's 1844 result matched or trailed 1843 state showings, suggesting ex-Whigs left Clay earlier.

sources.title: Liberty Party (United States, 1840)

findings.claim: A popular-history site says most Liberty voters were Whig defectors and Clay would have won with half of them.

sources.title: Third Party Voting and the 1844 Election : We're History

findings.claim: Liberty voters were mostly ex-Whigs early (two-thirds to three-quarters in Connecticut 1841-43), but after 1842 many antislavery Democrats joined and eventually predominated; Morris was a former Democrat.

sources.title: Liberty Party (United States, 1840)

caveats: Liberty actually ran in 1844; all claims are inference, no study models its absence.

before.quote: The man from Ohio speaks sense about not favoring factories over farming. We don't need the government taking our money for a national bank neither.
before.reason: Harry Ellis is a property-owning farmer in Indiana who meets voting requirements and lives in an agricultural region where Polk's opposition to federal favoritism and protective tariffs aligns with rural interests. His age and settled circumstances suggest he votes regularly, though the tariff question creates some uncertainty between the candidates.

after.quote: The Democrat's our man—he stands against the banks and that protective tariff that hurts us farmers. And Texas and Oregon belong to us by rights.
after.reason: Harry Ellis is a property-owning farmer in Indiana who meets the state's voting qualifications. As an older man of means in rural Indiana, he likely sympathizes with the Democratic nominee's opposition to a national bank and protective tariffs that would burden agricultural interests, and his expansionist platform appeals to western sentiment.

before.quote: The tariff keeps the mills running and wages up. That's what matters to a working man like me. Though I confess this Texas business worries me some.

before.quote: I'll vote for the man who won't let the banks and merchants run the government for their own gain. The tariff question troubles me some, but at least he won't charter a national bank to bleed working men.
before.reason: Harry Tate works for wages in a mill or workshop, making him sensitive to tariff policy and currency stability. Polk's opposition to federal favoritism toward industry and rejection of a national bank align with a working man's suspicion of banking interests, while Clay's protective tariff might seem to benefit manufacturers more than laborers. The Oregon and Texas questions are distant concerns compared to bread-and-butter economics.

after.quote: The Texas question stirs men up something fierce. I mind the tariff more—it makes everything cost more. I'll likely vote the Democrat way, but Mister Clay has his points too.
after.reason: Harry Tate is a working man earning wages in Illinois, without deep ties to either major party faction. He likely leans toward Polk's opposition to a national bank and protective tariffs that would raise prices on goods he buys, and toward expansion which appeals to his generation's ambitions, though he is uncertain enough to leave significant room for the Whig alternative or abstention.

before.quote: This Texas business needs settling, and the tariff's been a weight on working men. The man from Ohio talks sense on that score.

after.quote: The man from Tennessee knows what the West needs—Texas and Oregon both. A tariff that raises prices on what we buy don't help a mill hand like me, but land and growth do.
after.reason: James Hayes works for wages in rural Arkansas and would benefit from the expansionist program of territorial growth promised by Polk, particularly Texas annexation which could open new lands and economic opportunity. Clay's protective tariff stance offers less appeal to a working man in an agricultural state.
